barnum-effect.summary: People are willing to believe vague descriptions that seem “spot on” for them.
barnum-effect.plain: Vague, flattering descriptions that apply to almost anyone feel as if they were tailored to you personally.
barnum-effect.example: Horoscopes and quick personality quizzes say things like “you are sometimes outgoing, sometimes reserved,” and everyone finds it accurate.
barnum-effect.misuse: This does not mean all personality tests are the same. It is a reminder that feeling accurate is not evidence of validity.

social-desirability.summary: When answering questionnaires, people tend to give answers that make them look good.
social-desirability.plain: On self-report items, people tend to choose answers that present themselves favorably, whether consciously or not.
social-desirability.example: Asked “Would you cheat to win?” most people answer “No.”
social-desirability.misuse: This does not mean “everyone is lying.” It shows that purely self-reported measures need other evidence to back them up.

learning-styles.summary: Claims like “I am a visual learner” lack supporting evidence.
learning-styles.plain: The idea that each person has a preferred way of receiving information, and that matching teaching to that preference leads to better learning, has not been supported in controlled experiments.
learning-styles.example: Students labeled “visual learners” who were shown only diagrams, and “auditory learners” who were only lectured to, did not perform better as a result.
learning-styles.misuse: This is one of the most widely believed education myths. Preferences are real, but there is no evidence that teaching to a preference makes learning more effective.

effect-size.summary: How large an effect is, not just whether it exists.
effect-size.plain: Statistical significance only says that a difference is unlikely to be pure chance. Effect size tells you how large the difference is.
effect-size.example: A method that raises average scores by only 0.1 points can be “significant” with a large enough sample, yet have almost no practical meaning.
effect-size.misuse: Often overlooked. Many news reports say a result is “significant” without saying how large the effect is.

preregistration.summary: Writing down hypotheses and the analysis plan before doing the study.
preregistration.plain: Publicly registering a research plan before collecting data makes it hard to “manufacture significance” afterward by changing the hypothesis or switching analyses.
preregistration.example: A researcher states in advance, “I will compare groups A and B on outcome 2.” Afterward, only that result is reported, and the other analyses are labeled as exploratory.
preregistration.misuse: This does not mean exploratory research has no value. It simply asks researchers to separate exploration from testing.

trait-state.summary: Stable tendencies must be distinguished from momentary states.
trait-state.plain: A trait is a long-lasting tendency that holds across situations. A state is how you feel and act at a given moment. The two are different.
trait-state.example: A usually calm person feels anxious before an exam today. This is state anxiety and does not necessarily mean high trait anxiety.
trait-state.misuse: A common mistake is treating the result of a single measurement as proof that “this is simply who you are.”

assimilation-accommodation.summary: Understanding something new through an existing framework, or changing the framework to fit it.
assimilation-accommodation.plain: When new information fits into existing ideas, this is assimilation. When it does not fit, the ideas must be revised, and that is accommodation.
assimilation-accommodation.example: A child who first sees a cat calls it a “dog” (assimilation). After being corrected, the child creates a new category for “cat” (accommodation).
assimilation-accommodation.misuse: Often memorized as a pair of terms, while the key point is overlooked: the drive to learn comes from the imbalance between the two.

conservation.summary: Understanding that the amount stays the same even when the shape changes.
conservation.plain: Grasping that an object's quantity, volume and similar properties do not change just because its appearance does.
conservation.example: When the same amount of water is poured into a tall, thin glass, young children say there is “more.” Around age seven, most children understand that the amount is the same.
conservation.misuse: This is not a sign that “earlier is smarter.” It is a milestone in cognitive development, and the age at which children reach it varies quite a bit across cultures.

object-permanence.summary: Knowing that a hidden object still exists.
object-permanence.plain: Understanding that objects continue to exist even when we cannot see them. Piaget thought this emerged around eight months, while later experiments suggest it appears earlier.
object-permanence.example: In peekaboo, a very young baby seems to think Mom has “vanished.” An older child will look for her.
object-permanence.misuse: The claim that “babies only get this at a few months old” depends on how it is measured. It is not a fixed age.

secure-base.summary: A child uses the caregiver as a starting point for exploring.
secure-base.plain: The child knows they can return to the caregiver when something is difficult, and that knowledge gives them the confidence to venture out and explore.
secure-base.example: A one-year-old playing in a park glances back at Mom now and then, then runs off to play again.
secure-base.misuse: Often misunderstood as “clinging all the time.” Children with secure attachment are actually more willing to be independent.

attachment-styles.summary: Several common ways of relating intimately, from infancy into adult relationships.
attachment-styles.plain: Stable tendencies in what people expect from close relationships, such as secure, anxious and avoidant. They are best seen as dimensions along a continuum, and they can change.
attachment-styles.example: An anxiously attached person constantly worries that a partner has not replied to a message. An avoidantly attached person pulls away as a relationship grows closer.
attachment-styles.misuse: The most common misuse is treating it as a lifelong label, slapping a type onto yourself or others and treating that as settled.

identity-crisis.summary: A period when the question “Who am I?” becomes especially pressing.
identity-crisis.plain: Adolescents and young adults often explore and wrestle with their values, roles and future direction.
identity-crisis.example: After graduating from university, someone is unsure what they want to do and dissatisfied with the status quo, so they keep trying new things and questioning their choices.
identity-crisis.misuse: Often treated as an illness. Erikson saw it as a normal developmental task, and handled well, it leads to a clearer sense of self.

false-belief.summary: Understanding that what others believe may differ from the facts.
false-belief.plain: Recognizing that someone else's belief may be wrong, and that they will act on that wrong belief.
false-belief.example: You tell a friend the party is at restaurant A, then it is moved to B. You understand that your friend will go to A first.
false-belief.misuse: This is not the same as empathy. It is a cognitive ability to understand what others think, and it does not involve whether you care about them.

egocentrism.summary: Difficulty seeing things from another person's point of view.
egocentrism.plain: Piaget described young children as finding it hard to imagine that others see things differently from themselves. Later research found that children do better in familiar situations.
egocentrism.example: A young child nods in response to a phone call, because they assume the other person can see them.
egocentrism.misuse: This is not the same as selfishness. It means that cognitively, a child cannot temporarily step outside their own point of view.

temperament.summary: Innate styles of reacting, such as being easily aroused or easily calmed.
temperament.plain: Differences present from birth in the intensity of reactions, the speed of adapting and the basic emotional tone. They have some genetic basis and are also shaped by the environment.
temperament.example: Some babies cry and fuss in a new environment, while others eat and sleep as usual.
temperament.misuse: The claim that “children are simply born that way” is an oversimplification. Temperament and parenting interact.

diffusion-of-responsibility.summary: The more people present, the less responsible each person feels.
diffusion-of-responsibility.plain: When many people are around, each one assumes that someone else will take care of it, and as a result, no one acts.
diffusion-of-responsibility.example: Someone collapses in an elevator, and the people there look at each other, each waiting for someone else to speak up first.
diffusion-of-responsibility.misuse: This does not prove that “human nature is cold.” Clearly asking one specific person for help usually breaks the pattern.

groupthink.summary: In the pursuit of unity, a group stops rigorously testing its decisions.
groupthink.plain: Highly cohesive groups that crave agreement may suppress dissent and make very risky decisions.
groupthink.example: Everyone nods in a meeting, no one raises objections, and only later does it become clear that the plan had obvious flaws.
groupthink.misuse: As an explanatory model, it draws mostly on case analyses after the fact, and experimental support is limited. It should not be treated as a law that always applies.

in-group-bias.summary: A preference for members of the group you belong to.
in-group-bias.plain: When judging, allocating resources and evaluating, people tend to favor members of their own group.
in-group-bias.example: People from the same hometown, school or sports team more easily win trust and help.
in-group-bias.misuse: This is not the same as hostility toward outsiders. Often it simply means being better to one's own group, not worse to others.

social-proof.summary: Looking at what others do to decide what you should do.
social-proof.plain: When uncertain, people treat others' behavior as a clue to what is correct.
social-proof.example: If a restaurant has a line at the door, you assume the food must be good.
social-proof.misuse: Do not confuse it with the “identity” in social identity theory. Here it means using others' behavior as a reference, not a sense of belonging.

foot-in-the-door.summary: Agreeing to a small request makes it easier to agree to a larger one.
foot-in-the-door.plain: Once someone agrees to a small request, they are more likely to agree to a bigger one later, because they want to stay consistent with their earlier behavior.
foot-in-the-door.example: You are first asked to sign a petition, and later asked to donate. The success rate is higher than asking for the donation directly.
foot-in-the-door.misuse: The size of the effect varies with the situation. It is not a magic formula that makes any sales pitch work.

self-serving-bias.summary: Credit success to yourself, blame failure on circumstances.
self-serving-bias.plain: People tend to attribute success to their own ability and failure to external factors.
self-serving-bias.example: “I did well on the exam because I'm smart. I did badly because the questions were unfair.”
self-serving-bias.misuse: The effect is weaker in some East Asian contexts, and it is not universal. In people with depression, it can even be reversed.

stereotype.summary: A simplified generalization about a category of people.
stereotype.plain: Summarizing features believed to belong to a group, and then applying them to infer things about each individual in it.
stereotype.example: Believing that “science students are all bad at socializing,” and forming an opinion of a particular science student before you even meet them.
stereotype.misuse: Stereotypes do not require prejudice to exist. They are a by-product of the mind's effort-saving shortcuts, but they can lead to unfair judgments.

individualism-collectivism.summary: Whether a society emphasizes the individual or the group.
individualism-collectivism.plain: One cultural dimension: individualist cultures value personal goals and autonomy, while collectivist cultures value group harmony and responsibility.
individualism-collectivism.example: “Be yourself” is often encouraged in the United States, while in many East Asian families one is expected to consider what family members think.
individualism-collectivism.misuse: It is wrong to use it to label every individual. There is great variation within any culture, and behavior changes with the situation.

self-fulfilling.summary: Because you believe something will happen, you make it happen.
self-fulfilling.plain: An expectation that was not necessarily correct to begin with guides a person's behavior, and in the end makes the expectation come true.
self-fulfilling.example: You believe you will fail the job interview, so you get nervous and perform poorly, and you do indeed fail.
self-fulfilling.misuse: This is not “thinking something makes it so.” The expectation only works through behavior.

unconditional-positive-regard.summary: Acceptance that does not depend on how you perform.
unconditional-positive-regard.plain: Accepting a person as they are, without the condition that they must meet your demands. This does not mean approving of every behavior.
unconditional-positive-regard.example: A child does poorly on a test, and a parent first says, “I can see you're really upset,” rather than, “Why didn't you study harder?”
unconditional-positive-regard.misuse: Often misunderstood as “unconditional agreement” or “never setting limits.” Rogers meant accepting the person, not endorsing every behavior.

intrinsic-motivation.summary: Doing something because the activity itself is interesting.
intrinsic-motivation.plain: Doing something out of interest, curiosity and a sense of accomplishment, rather than for a reward or to avoid punishment.
intrinsic-motivation.example: Doing puzzles or writing code not for money, but simply because it is fun.
intrinsic-motivation.misuse: “Intrinsic” does not mean “no outside support is needed.” An environment that supports autonomy, competence and connection greatly influences it.

meaning-in-life.summary: Feeling that life has purpose, matters and makes sense.
meaning-in-life.plain: It has three parts: life feels coherent, it has direction and goals, and one's own life matters.
meaning-in-life.example: Caring for children, committing to work, faith and creative work can all give a sense of meaning.
meaning-in-life.misuse: Meaning should not become a single answer one must find, and it is not something to demand from someone in the middle of suffering.

existential-givens.summary: Death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness: four things no one can avoid.
existential-givens.plain: Yalom's list of life conditions: we will die, we must make choices and take responsibility for them, we are fundamentally alone, and the world does not supply meaning on its own.
existential-givens.example: The death of a loved one, a major choice, or facing the quiet of a solitary night can each bring these facts into focus.
existential-givens.misuse: This does not mean pessimism. Existential therapy holds that facing these facts can help people live more authentically.

peak-experience.summary: A brief, intense moment of meaningful experience.
peak-experience.plain: Moments in which a person feels especially whole, joyful and connected to the world, such as while climbing a mountain, listening to music or in moments of love.
peak-experience.example: The awe and stillness of watching the sunrise from a mountaintop.
peak-experience.misuse: Often treated as a goal that can be achieved by pursuing it. In fact, it usually arrives by chance, as a by-product.

hedonic-eudaimonic.summary: Well-being comes in two kinds: feeling good and living meaningfully.
hedonic-eudaimonic.plain: Hedonic well-being emphasizes pleasure and satisfaction. Eudaimonic well-being emphasizes growth, meaning and realizing one's potential.
hedonic-eudaimonic.example: Enjoying a fine meal is the first kind. Working toward something important over many years is the second.
hedonic-eudaimonic.misuse: The two are not opposites, and neither should be treated as “higher” than the other.

autotelic.summary: The activity is its own reward.
autotelic.plain: Doing something is satisfying in itself, without needing an external reason.
autotelic.example: Some people will spend hours playing chess, playing the piano or climbing mountains simply because the activity absorbs them.
autotelic.misuse: Not everything that is fun is autotelic. The activity needs to match one's abilities with a suitable challenge.

empty-chair.summary: Speaking to an empty chair as if a person were sitting in it, to say what was left unsaid.
empty-chair.plain: A therapy technique: you imagine the other person in the chair and say the feelings you never expressed, or switch roles and answer as that person.
empty-chair.example: A person who lost their mother speaks to an empty chair: “I miss you so much,” and “I was really angry with you back then.”
empty-chair.misuse: It is not a performance. Its purpose is to let suppressed emotions come out, and it should be used with a trained therapist present.

unconscious.summary: Mental processes that are outside awareness but still shape behavior.
unconscious.plain: Much of our perception, motivation and judgment happens without our noticing. Modern cognitive science has amply confirmed this, though its content differs from Freud's account.
unconscious.example: You feel an unexplained dislike toward someone and cannot say why. In fact, they may remind you of someone from your past.
unconscious.misuse: Often mythologized as a place “full of secrets.” In reality, most unconscious processing is automatic and ordinary.

defense-mechanism.summary: Mental strategies people use, often without awareness, to reduce anxiety.
defense-mechanism.plain: Ways of coping that people use without realizing it when faced with thoughts or feelings they cannot easily bear, such as denial, rationalization and displacement.
defense-mechanism.example: After being criticized, you immediately say, “He was just out to get me” (projection), or you make a joke to deflect the pain (humor).
defense-mechanism.misuse: The most common misuse is using it to “diagnose” other people. If someone rejects your view, they are called “defensive,” and that makes them impossible to argue with.

projection.summary: Attributing your own emotions or traits to other people.
projection.plain: Seeing in others the emotions or traits you do not want to admit in yourself.
projection.example: You envy a colleague but keep feeling that the colleague envies you.
projection.misuse: Often misused as a debate tactic: “You say I am like this, but really you are the one who is like this.”
